sources.headline: The Trump coalition is shattered - what will Republicans do now?
sources.text: Image source, Getty ImagesByDaniel BushWashington correspondent and Madeline HalpertRepublicans are in soul-searching mode after the coalition that powered Donald Trump to three straight presidential nominations imploded in spectacular fashion in the 2026 midterms.The stunning election defeat immediately raised questions about the party's future post-Trump.But there are no easy answers as Republicans face the choice of doubling down on Trumpism or trying to chart a new path forward in his final years in office.The depth of the problem was captured by outgoing Florida Governor Ron DeSantis, who called the midterms "close to an extinction-level event for Republicans".Others struck a more optimistic tone. Vice-President JD Vance, who blamed the midterm results on public anger over the war with Iran, argued the party could turn things around. Nevertheless Vance acknowledged the fallout will be messy."There will be a lot of infighting and arguing over what happened and why," Vance said.The wide range of reactions on the right highlights deep fault lines in the party that formed around Trump's improbable rise to the presidency in 2016 and never really went away. It's too early to tell which faction will win. But while Republicans are still licking their wounds, the intraparty battle Vance predicted is already under way.The party must decide whether it will be "centred on one figure, one guy, or on a wider set of ideas like conservatism that can win outside the deepest red places," Rina Shah, a Republican strategist, told the BBC.Critics on the right - the "Never Trumpers" who opposed his first White House campaign - are pushing for a return to the Republican Party's pre-Trump roots, citing the historic losses around the country on election night.But simply turning back the clock on Trump will be extremely difficult if not impossible to do.The party has been wholly transformed during Trump's decade-long reign. Most Republicans have shifted to the right on domestic issues like immigration, and rejected the interventionist foreign policy of the George W Bush era that led to the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan.In Congress, the more moderate establishment wing of the party that disliked Trump from the start has almost entirely disappeared, replaced by conservative Trump backers who echo his nativism and populist rhetoric.That trend continued this year, as old-guard Republicans like John Cornyn in Texas and Maine's Susan Collins, both of whom clashed with Trump over the years, were voted out of office.Three days after the election Trump appointed Stephen Miller as his new White House chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles.The move signalled Trump has no plans to moderate his policies or message in his remaining years in office. Miller, who had been serving as the president's chief domestic policy adviser, is a longtime Trump aide known for his hardline immigration policies.One of the architects of the Make America Great Again (Maga) movement, Steve Bannon, predicted a "civil war" in the party after the midterms.Afterwards, he blamed the Republicans' defeat on the economy and "foreign wars". "I don't think we implemented the Maga programme," he said, calling on Trump to double down on mass deportations.But other Republican strategists said the midterms were a wake up call for Make America Great Again (Maga) loyalists who want Trump's political movement to outlast his presidency."There's still plenty of Maga voters out there who have supported Donald Trump through thick and thin," said Whit Ayres, a Republican strategist. "But there is also a significant portion of the Republican Party that's non-Maga, and that's a majority now."Image source, Getty ImagesShould Republican hopefuls distance themselves from Trump?The party lost control of the House and Senate, as well as governorships and state legislatures in red states like Texas and Kansas where Democrats had been shut out of power for decades - and where Trump won by double digits when he was on the ballot.The stunning upsets underscored the fickle nature of political coalitions.Trump expanded the Republican base in 2024, increasing support with Latinos and younger voters among other key groups. Republicans hailed the gains as a sign of future strength for the party.Just two years later, the party lost ground with nearly every critical voting bloc. According to a New York Times analysis of voter data, Latino support for Democratic candidates increased by 29 percentage points from 2024-26. Support from young voters 18-29 years old increased by 33 points.The swings reflected polling ahead of the midterms that found widespread disapproval with Trump's handling of the economy, immigration and the war with Iran.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Tuesday night saw Trump's Republicans lose in states they had comfortably held for decadesDemocrats also capitalised on a public perception that the Trump family and administration is rife with self-dealing and corruption. The president's focus on the White House ballroom and other Washington construction projects also contributed to a sense among voters that he was more focused on his legacy than addressing affordability issues.It's a sentiment shared by Benjamin Shrader, the leader of the Young Republicans in Austin, who was still shell-shocked when he spoke to the BBC in Texas the morning after his party was almost wiped out in the state by a Democratic "blue tsunami".Shrader said Trump was still a "force of nature" when asked to reflect on how the president had used his first public appearance after the results to show off the White House ballroom project.He hesitated before adding: "I would focus on issues that are not ballrooms, that are not renaming things. I would focus on what matters."The evidence in the immediate aftermath of the midterms suggests that Republicans could benefit by distancing themselves from Trump ahead of 2028.Figure caption, With Congress flipped, what does Donald Trump do next?'Vance was the favourite - now the race is wide open'Vance tried to thread the needle with his midterm assessment blaming the Iran war and calling for a return to "America First." It was a nuanced critique that broke with Trump on an unpopular war, but embraced a broader political brand that remains popular with the Maga base.Trump's next moves on Iran will be watched closely by the party for their 2028 implications. An escalation would risk fuelling the concerns voiced by Vance and other "America First" proponents.In his postmortem statement on X, Vance also echoed the growing calls on the right to reexamine US support for Israel. But he also signalled an openness to making some immigration enforcement changes. That clashes with Miller, a Vance ally who has speared the administration's second-term immigration agenda.Party strategists said the midterm drubbing complicated Vance's path to the nomination."Before this midterm, JD Vance was the odds-on favourite to win the Republican nomination in 2028. After this midterm, the nomination battle is completely wide open," Ayres said.Potential Trump successors have some time to consider their options, but they'll have to make up their minds relatively soon. Any 2028 presidential hopefuls will face pressure to announce White House bids in the next few months. Some could launch campaigns before the end of the year.Vance's election analysis was widely interpreted as an unofficial signal of his plans to run. It will likely be a crowded primary field.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Both Vice-President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio are seen as contenders for the 2028 nominationOther rumoured White House contenders include Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Senator Ted Cruz of Texas, Florida Governor DeSantis, former US ambassador to the United Nations Nikki Haley and former New Jersey Governor Chris Christie, to name a few.In the next election cycle, Republican presidential and congressional candidates alike will have tough decisions to make on key issues of the day, from US support for Israel to tariffs to the AI boom.Trump's power may be diminished as he enters the final two years of his second term, but he'll still have the loudest voice in the party over the next two years. It's unclear whether he will get deeply involved in the process or take a hands-off approach.Trump has praised Vance and Rubio at different times, but typically deflects questions about who he'd like to see succeed him.His endorsement will loom as the biggest wildcard in the 2028 Republican primary race."It remains to be seen who will jump into that race," Ayres said."But I think it's going to be a lot larger and more diverse than we anticipated before the midterm election."Figure caption, 'Hopefully things get done': Americans react to historic political shiftFollow the twists and turns of Trump's second term with North America correspondent Anthony Zurcher's US Politics Unspun newsletter. sources.headline: After the midterms, where does the Republican Party stand?
sources.text: On Tuesday, the United States held midterm elections. Every one of the 435 seats in the US House of Representatives was up for election and 35 of the 100 US Senate seats were on the ballot.The result of the elections was overwhelmingly in favour of the Democratic Party, or the blue team, as the US media has taken to referring to them. It was a blue wave. A blue tsunami. Democrats flipped at least 40 House seats and seven Senate seats. It was a clear message to Washington that much of the US is unhappy with the direction the country is headed.Texas had not elected a Democrat in a statewide race for more than 30 years. Democrats dominated in Texas. Kansas hadn’t sent a Democrat to the Senate since 1932. Come the first week of January, there will be one representing it. Susan Collins, the powerful Republican chair of the Senate Committee on Appropriations and the most bipartisan voting Republican in the US Senate had been Maine’s senator for 30 years. She was voted out. The depth and breadth of the Democratic victory stunned many.The war with Iran clearly had an impact. It wasn’t the conflict itself nearly as much as the economic impact it has had on the average American. Virtually every American uses an automobile and the price of petrol has skyrocketed during the war. The high fuel prices have impacted every other segment of the economy because nearly every product, especially food and grocery items, is delivered using the roadway system, which, of course, means petrol and diesel prices add to their cost.The Democrats taking control of both the House and the Senate will dramatically change the next two years in Washington. They will restore the oversight functions of Congress and will investigate Trump and his team for countless violations, real or imagined. Congressional priorities will change. Impeachment will be a word that is commonly used again. If a vacancy occurs on the Supreme Court, the president will have a much more difficult time filling it. The impact of the elections is very real.Is it historic though? In a word, no.Losing seats to the opposition party is actually quite common in the midterms. Dozens of House races are still being counted, so the final tally may yet grow, but since World War II there have been at least seven midterm elections with seat losses comparable to or larger than what the Republicans have experienced so far in 2026: 1946, 1958, 1966, 1974, 1994, 2010 and 2018 when President Donald Trump’s party lost about 40 House seats in his first midterm.The largest midterm loss belongs to President Barack Obama’s party in 2010. The Democrats lost 63 House seats and six seats in the Senate. The Democrats would then lose nine seats in the US Senate in the midterm elections held during Obama’s second term.The Democrats under President Bill Clinton also took a beating in 1994 when the opposition Republicans gained 54 seats in the House, taking a majority for the first time in a generation, and flipping eight seats in the Senate.The pundits at the time wondered aloud if it was the end of the Democratic Party. The losses were staggering. Both presidents, however, went on to govern effectively and find ways to work with the opposition. In fact, Clinton worked with the Republican Congress to pass the first balanced budget in memory. In that case, the split in government forced them to work together and produced a benefit to the American people.None of this is new. President Harry Truman’s Democrats lost 55 House seats and 12 Senate seats in 1946. President Dwight Eisenhower’s Republicans took it on the chin in 1958, losing 48 House seats and 13 Senate seats. Presidents Lyndon Johnson, Gerald Ford and George HW Bush all took big losses. Even Ronald Reagan lost 26 House seats in his first midterm elections.The point is the American public has always demanded accountability from Washington. No one should be surprised that at a time when only 14 percent of Americans think Congress is doing a good job and the prices for basic necessities are increasing, Americans demand change. They have done it over and over, regardless of the party in power.The next logical question is where do we go from here? Is Trump’s reign as leader of the GOP over? Has he lost his influence?There will not be a great deal of time spent trying to decipher what went wrong. Both Trump and Vice President JD Vance have already acknowledged the war in Iran and its economic effects are the primary reasons for the loss. This acknowledgement will hasten the healing process within the party, as will the need to push through a number of agenda items together in the remaining weeks the Republicans have control of Congress.Because the US Constitution limits a president to two terms, any time any president enters his final two years, he is known as a lame duck. His influence, while still enormous simply by the reality of the office, begins to wane. The closer it gets to the end of his final term the less influence he has, particularly on the domestic agenda. Many presidents spend the majority of their time near the end of their term on foreign policy.As of January 3, Democrats will set the agenda on Capitol Hill. They will control every committee. They will control virtually every vote. Congress controls the purse strings, so their impact is large, but don’t count Trump out yet.His personality and his outward embrace of even the most difficult conflicts are unique. Whether in business, in election wins and losses, in courtroom clashes or in international affairs, Trump doesn’t back down. Admittedly this sometimes works to his detriment, but it is a trait that will likely serve him well as he battles with a Democratic-controlled Congress.The president has veto authority over any legislation Congress passes. Rather than sign the legislation, he can reject it. If he rejects it, two-thirds of both the House and the Senate must vote to override his veto or else the legislation does not become law.If Trump feels the Democrats are pushing an agenda too radical or too far left, he will wield the veto pen with great regularity.Ideally the two sides understand the power each holds, and they will work together, as did a Republican-dominated Congress and Democratic President Clinton. If they do work together, all Americans will benefit. If each side digs in and refuses to compromise, it will be a long, unproductive two years.Speaking of two years, 2028 is the next presidential election, and the question of who will be the nominee for each party is already being kicked around – and, in particular, how these midterm elections will impact the potential Republican candidates like Vance or Secretary of State Marco Rubio.The stark reality is that two years is an eternity in politics. Anything can happen, despite the Republican defeat on Tuesday. The biggest question is whether the American public will be feeling “Trump fatigue” during the 2028 presidential election season.If the public has grown weary of team Trump, anyone affiliated with his administration may be tainted goods and face a bigger challenge getting the party’s nomination. Vance, Rubio and others directly tied to him have the greatest name recognition right now, but that may prove to be baggage rather than an advantage.Outsiders such as a state governor or a past political figure may generate public enthusiasm for a different direction. The list is long. Even Trump has said his party has a deep bench, and it’s true.Trying to predict the 2028 nominee now, in such a volatile political time and with two years to go, while entertaining, is a fool’s errand.Some in the media have begun to write the Republican Party’s obituary after Tuesday’s losses. The final numbers are not yet in, and in the Senate, the seven seats already lost exceed the six Obama’s party gave up in 2010.Still, history shows that parties and presidents have come back from setbacks of this scale before, as Obama and Clinton both did. Trump and the Republicans can do the same.A version of this piece was first published by Al Jazeera Arabic.The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

sources.headline: ‘Trump has cost us’: After midterm losses, MAGA asks if it’s over
sources.text: DALLAS – As Republicans faced a nationwide drubbing in the Nov 3 midterm elections, supporters streamed out of a Dallas ballroom where they had hoped to toast a win for US Senate candidate Ken Paxton, a favourite of President Donald Trump.In the hotel bar, Michael Little, a 59-year-old businessman and three-time Trump voter, stared at the president’s image on a television screen.“People are pissed off at Trump. Trump has cost us,” he said, capturing a sentiment rippling through the president’s Make America Great Again (MAGA) movement after the Republican Party’s worst electoral defeat in decades.Across the coalition, some supporters who once viewed Trump as MAGA’s greatest asset are beginning to question whether he has become its biggest liability.Still, the midterm losses amounted to more than a repudiation of Trump. They were a referendum on the political and cultural movement he built.A defining force in American politics that began as a campaign slogan during Trump’s 2016 presidential run now faces a potentially existential reckoning after voters disillusioned with soaring fuel prices, the Iran war and Washington corruption delivered Democrats decisive congressional majorities.Trump’s first major response to the midterms came on Nov 6.Instead of changing course, he doubled down on the movement’s core. He promoted Stephen Miller, the main architect of the administration’s hardline immigration crackdown, to chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles. Wiles was seen as a stabilising force inside an often chaotic White House.The move was celebrated by some of MAGA’s most ardent influencers, who saw it as a return to the anti-immigration agenda at the movement’s roots. “Exactly the energy we need,” right-wing influencer Benny Johnson posted on X to his 4.1 million followers. “Solid move. It’s Miller Time.”The White House did not directly answer Reuters’ questions about why Republicans lost, the defeat of candidates who embraced Trump’s false 2020 election claims, or where MAGA goes from here.Instead, it pointed to Trump’s remarks on Nov 4, when he said, “If I were on the ballot, we would have won.” He also said it was “largely true” that the Iran war had cost Republicans because “it drove the gasoline up”, but that he would do it again.For nearly a decade, MAGA has reshaped the Republican Party and transformed national debates on issues such as trade, immigration, race and gender. The movement installed loyalists throughout federal agencies, cracked down on immigration and pressured corporations and public institutions to retreat from diversity, equity and inclusion initiatives.MAGA survived the fallout from the Jan 6, 2021, attack on the US Capitol and propelled Trump back to the White House. Now, the Democrats’ sweeping victory has forced the movement to grapple with an unexpected question: Is MAGA over?Reuters interviews with more than a dozen MAGA activists, influencers, party strategists, Christian nationalist leaders and researchers who track right-wing politics, along with a review of MAGA supporters’ posts and podcasts since Nov 3, show a movement turning its anger on itself.The stolen-election claims that have driven MAGA since Democrat Joe Biden beat Trump in the 2020 presidential election have mostly gone quiet. Instead, supporters are blaming Republican leaders and Trump's advisers, and in some cases the President himself, for broken promises on living costs, the Iran war and the government’s decision to redact or withhold major portions of its investigative files on late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.MAGA’s factions also disagree about what comes next. Some want a return to populist and nationalist basics. Some want a movement less tied to one man. And a vocal minority say MAGA is already dead.“We have to rebuild,” Steve Bannon, a prominent MAGA proponent, podcaster and former Trump White House adviser, told Reuters. He urged the party to double down on an aggressive populist and nationalist agenda, and praised Trump for elevating Miller.“Miller’s appointment as chief of staff underpins my point,” he said. “There is no more hardcore MAGA proponent than Stephen.”As pro-Trump internet forums digested the election results, a notable slice of self-described MAGA loyalists – more than 20% – raised doubts about the movement’s leadership and direction, according to an analysis of social media traffic done for Reuters by PeakMetrics, a data intelligence firm.About half of that cohort remained supportive of the MAGA movement but no longer backed Trump as its leader. The other half remained loyal to, though critical of, the President himself.The analysis was based on 12,850 posts sampled from a universe of 4.6 million Trump-related comments on X and Reddit from 9pm on Election Day to 8pm the next evening. It found broad concern among MAGA supporters as the results became clear.Of the posts that assigned blame for the rout, nearly a third said concerns about the Iran war and Israel’s influence over US policy had overshadowed Trump’s message. A quarter said Republicans not fully committed to the MAGA agenda had undermined the movement.The results left Trump facing large Democratic majorities in both chambers of Congress. In the Senate, Democrats could control as many as 56 of the chamber’s 100 seats, more than enough to block Trump’s future judicial picks. Republicans might not be able to recapture the Senate until 2032, Florida Governor Ron DeSantis said the morning after the election.“It’s the political equivalent of a meteor strike that went all around the United States,” DeSantis, a Republican, said at a post-election briefing.Democrats will now control governorships in seven battleground states Trump won in 2024 and, strikingly, they won every statewide race in Texas, which has not backed a Democratic presidential candidate since 1976.‘MAGA is stale’Since Nov 3, talk of election fraud has virtually vanished among right-wing influencers.“I have been banging the drum of rigged and stolen elections since 2020, but that is not why we lost the midterms,” Rogan O’Handley, a MAGA influencer who posts under the name DC_Draino, wrote on X to his 2.3 million followers. “We lost because we failed to fix the things voters sent us to do.” He did not respond to a request for comment.After the 2020 election, Trump supporter Isabella DeLuca was among thousands who stormed the US Capitol on Jan 6, 2021. She was charged with five crimes, including theft of a table from inside the Capitol, and pleaded not guilty. Her case was dismissed after Trump returned to office and pardoned her.This time, the 26-year-old conservative influencer directed her anger towards what she described as out-of-touch Republican leaders who failed to appeal to Gen Z voters on affordability, avoiding foreign wars and other key issues.“Republicans were just lazy. They felt like that they were entitled to people’s votes and that people would vote for them no matter what,” DeLuca told Reuters. “It goes to show you that you do have to earn people’s votes, and that even in a super-red state like Texas, you're not untouchable.”The MAGA movement this year appeared “tired”, she said.That sentiment was echoed in online right-wing forums, said Jennifer Golbeck, a University of Maryland professor who has analysed MAGA-related posts since 2016. She said engagement by Trump’s most loyal backers has steadily declined since January, including a 27% drop in posts and comments on Patriots.Win, a popular MAGA forum.“The enthusiasm and the passion even among this hardest core group of supporters hasn’t really been there,” Golbeck said. “They are saying that ‘MAGA is stale’. It’s not new and exciting like it once was.”Fox News, a cable network that has long been a key platform for MAGA voices, saw a sharp decline in viewership ahead of the midterms, with its total daytime audience down 27% in October from a year earlier, according to Nielsen, the audience measurement firm.In a statement to Reuters, Fox said it drew more viewers than its cable-news rivals on election night. “Fox News has been the number one network in cable news for a quarter-century,” spokesperson Caley Cronin said.Some prominent right-wing influencers blamed the President’s advisers or Republican lawmakers – but rarely Trump himself – for ignoring key voter concerns. In posts, online broadcasts and interviews with Reuters, many blamed dissatisfaction with the economy, though they differed on other reasons for the Nov 3 results.It was not just failure to address affordability that “crushed” Republicans, said Ben Shapiro, co-founder of the conservative site Daily Wire, on his online show on Nov 4. “If you’re talking about an electoral catastrophe – a wipe-out like we saw last night – you need more ingredients. Here are the other ingredients: chaos and corruption.”Laura Loomer, an influencer close to Trump, wrote on X: “America is over and the American Dream is dead.” Yet, she told Reuters that the losses did not signal the end

Republicans face prospect of ‘civil war’ as Trump’s air of invincibility starts to fade

Traditional Republican China hawks may try to challenge the influence of the US president and his Maga allies after election disaster

5-MIN READ
4
Listen
Make SCMP preferred on Google
Khushboo RazdanandAlbee Zhangin Shanghai
Published: 10:00pm, 4 Nov 2026

In the weeks leading up to the midterm elections, US President Donald Trump displayed unwavering confidence in his star power, urging supporters to close their eyes and “pretend I’m on the ballot”.

But Tuesday night’s disastrous results for the Republicans – the first time in 20 years both houses of Congress have changed hands at the same time – have punctured the aura of invincibility that once shielded Trump and allowed him to keep potential critics in line with the threat that opposing him could end their careers.

According to analysts tracking the post-election fallout, the Republican Party is increasingly at risk of a power struggle between Trump’s supporters and more traditional establishment figures.

Feng Chucheng, founding partner of the consultancy Hutong Research, said the results showed Trump had become “growingly detached” from grass-roots voters squeezed by rising living costs, inflation, tariffs and the Iran war.

“It’s very likely there will be an internal civil war within the Republican Party, leading to the 2028 presidential race to determine whether or not the Republicans want to find an alternative to Donald Trump,” he said.

“Who are they going to endorse in 2028 for the Republican candidacy? Are they going to endorse [Vice-President] J.D. Vance, who is seen as a protege of Trump, who is seen as a Maga successor of Trump? Or are they going to go back to people more orthodox like [Secretary of State] Marco Rubio, for example?” Feng asked, pointing to Rubio’s bipartisan confirmation as a sign of his broader appeal.

Feng argued the perceived risks of challenging Trump had weakened, adding: “Because you saw a lot of people aligning with Donald Trump, you saw Donald Trump on the campaign trails in the final weeks of the midterm elections, campaigning for this, endorsing these Republican candidates, and they all lost.

“They will have to first figure out, why did we lose all these critical toss-up elections? … They have to figure out who to blame. And right now, it looks like it’s Trump and the Iranian wars that they’re going to blame for their losses in these battlefield states.”

Wei Zongyou, a professor at Fudan University’s Centre for American Studies in Shanghai, described the results as a “blue tsunami”, predicting that “the GOP [Republicans] will look for a scapegoat after this”.

He said the losses could embolden establishment Republicans and dissenters to challenge Trump’s authority, adding: “They will use this opportunity to build up their strength and wait for the right moment.”

The discontent, however, extends beyond the Republican establishment. Wei pointed to growing dissatisfaction within Trump’s own Make America Great Again movement, including among far-right conservatives and China hawks, over some of his decisions.

“His influence within the Republican Party will certainly decline,” he said, adding that more Republicans may begin to see Trump not as an electoral asset but as a “political liability”.

Denis Simon, from the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft, a think tank in Washington, agreed that the results seemed to have “considerably” weakened Trump’s control of the party.

He added the midterms “have created a potentially important opening” for the Republicans the president had marginalised and those who “believe the party has become too dependent on Trump’s narcissistic personal leadership”.

Trump has systematically sidelined both traditional conservatives such as ex-Congresswoman Liz Cheney and national-security hawks like former national security adviser John Bolton, ex-secretary of state Mike Pompeo and former ambassador to the United Nations Nikki Haley, treating them as political liabilities.

03:00
The global impact of the coming US midterm elections under Donald Trump

Simon added that a Republican revolt against “Trump’s political style and methods is not necessarily a revolt against Trump’s policy agenda”.

He said: “Now Republican politicians face a different question: is the cost of remaining associated with Trump greater than the cost of disagreeing with him?”

He outlined three possible forms of rebellion, saying Republicans could try to distance themselves from the president; lawmakers may try to oppose him on issues such as China, tariffs, Iran and congressional oversight; or leading figures could challenge his control over candidate selection in the run-up to the next round of elections.

Diao Daming, a professor at Renmin University in Beijing, argued that even if Republicans thought the defeat was down to Trump’s poor performance in office, “would they necessarily win without him? I think that is equally uncertain”.

Austin Strange, an associate professor of international relations at the University of Hong Kong, said some Republicans had been vocal about their “displeasure with certain policies or gestures that Trump has recently made regarding China”.

“The midterm results – and the widespread perception that Trump’s recent policies were electoral liabilities rather than assets – certainly won’t make such individuals less likely to publicly voice their views,” he said.

Strange also said many members of Congress were China hawks, adding: “There has been a clear, bipartisan trend towards depicting US-China relations on fundamentally competitive terms.”

But he argued the main foreign policy focus was likely to be elsewhere, saying: “So while the need to more effectively manage relations with China remains an important agenda acknowledged by many … it will probably continue to take a back seat for now.”

The election was the first time in 20 years that Republicans lost both the House and the Senate at the same time. Photo: AFP

Feng said he doubted that the China hawks would quickly regain real power within the party.

“These people, they are strategists. They are foreign-policy makers. They don’t have as much of an influence as someone coming from a Republican stronghold,” he said.

“John Bolton can say whatever he wants on TV shows with regard to Trump. Pompeo can say whatever he wants on TV shows with regard to Trump, but he will not really influence the electoral outcomes in that regard.”

He added that Trump now had less room for manoeuvre on China.

Once Democrats take control of Congress in January, they will be even less willing to let him use congressional China bills as bargaining chips in negotiations with Beijing. “That’s a net gain for Beijing,” he said.

Strange also said Republican lawmakers were likely to focus on their domestic priorities and would be unlikely to accommodate the president’s requests for flexibility on China legislation.

Sourabh Gupta of the Institute for China-America Studies framed the night as a defeat for neoconservatives and “defence-first” Republicans, with the balance inside the party shifting towards figures such as Vance or the former TV host Tucker Carson who are wary about nation-building and fighting wars abroad.

He was blunt about the prospects for the figures Trump had marginalised, arguing that “their brand of foreign policy is dead in the current Republican Party. Trump was the one who killed it before he got swept into his own misadventure.”

01:47
President Trump accuses China of US election interference in prime-time speech

Feng and other analysts also argued there was still life in the Maga movement.

“I would say it’s not about whether or not Maga can continue to ride on Trump after he finishes his term,” he said. “It’s more about whether or not the people that ride on Maga will continue to claim that they are still Maga when Trump is gone.”

Ali Wyne, an analyst from the International Crisis Group, said: “Obituaries for the movement would be premature.

“President Trump would not have won twice, and more decisively in 2024 than in 2016, had it not had deep roots in the American body politic. The midterm results demonstrate, however, that his grip on his core base is diminishing.

“It is difficult to imagine, moreover, that any Republican successor could come close to exerting a comparable grip or dominating the media environment as thoroughly.”

Meanwhile, Simon from the Quincy Institute argued: “Too soon to say dead. Can say mortally wounded.”

Khushboo Razdan

Does an electoral repudiation of Donald Trump also mark the beginning of MAGA’s decline? Delano D'Souza is pleased to welcome Ian Reifowitz, SUNY Distinguished Professor of Historical Studies at Empire State University, who describes the Republican defeat as “an absolute and complete repudiation” of the president. He connects voters’ economic frustrations with resentment over presidential enrichment, while questioning whether ideological differences between progressive and moderate Democrats proved decisive. Looking towards 2028, Reifowitz identifies a central Republican dilemma: “If JD Vance is the nominee, he can’t run against Donald Trump”, yet Trump himself may refuse to relinquish control of the party.

sources.headline: ‘Trump will be gone in two years’: Defeated Maine MAGA candidate Bobby Charles turns against president after election loss
sources.text: Bobby Charles promptly distances himself from Trump after election defeat.A Republican candidate who modelled his campaign on US President Donald Trump has distanced himself from the president following a crushing defeat in Maine's gubernatorial election, saying he was optimistic about the future because Trump would be leaving office in two years.Bobby Charles, who lost to Democrat Hannah Pingree in Tuesday's election (November 3), made the remarks in an interview with Politico after his defeat."It sounds a little ironic," Charles said. "But I am nevertheless optimistic for the future because Trump's going to be gone in two years."Charles had promised to govern Maine along the lines of Trump's administration. At the launch of his gubernatorial campaign, he had said: "If you liked the first 90 days of Trump, if you liked the first two weeks of Trump, you would love the first few weeks of my administration, because we are going to flip this thing on its head."The Republican had also sold Trump-inspired merchandise on his campaign website and supported the president's tariffs and hardline immigration policies.He had actively sought Trump's endorsement during the campaign and welcomed Vice President JD Vance's backing, describing it as a "wonderful thing".Republicans blame Trump for election lossesCharles' remarks come as Republicans face a major setback in the 2026 midterm elections, with Democrats winning control of both chambers of Congress and several gubernatorial races.The losses have triggered criticism within the Republican Party, with some officials blaming Trump and his administration for the party's poor performance."We are beyond candidate quality. It's a bloodbath," a senior Senate Republican official told Politico, adding, "Trump did this."A Republican operative involved in swing-state campaigns also blamed the administration's handling of key issues."The people in the White House didn't do anything to stop him from engaging on things that were actively making everything worse because he was ignoring what the voters were caring about," the operative said.The criticism comes amid voter concerns over rising costs, inflation and the US conflict with Iran.White House rejects blameThe White House, however, has refused to accept responsibility for the Republican losses.A White House official told The Daily Beast that the administration remained "defiant", arguing that Trump was not personally on the ballot."President Trump was not on the ballot, and it's proven that Trump voters show up when he is on the ballot," the official said.The official also blamed the quality of candidates and predicted that voters who supported Democrats would regret their decision once gas prices declined following a resolution to the Iran conflict.Trump himself has dismissed suggestions that his leadership contributed to the Republican setback."I wasn't on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE," he wrote on Truth Social.Vice President JD Vande posted a detailed analysis of the defeat. "The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night," he concluded.Who is Bobby Charles?Charles, a Republican and former assistant secretary of state under President George W. Bush, contested the Maine gubernatorial election against Democrat Hannah Pingree and independent candidate Rick Bennett.Pingree, a former speaker of the Maine House of Representatives and daughter of Democratic Congresswoman Chellie Pingree, won the race.Charles had built his campaign around Trump's political agenda, particularly immigration enforcement. He had even proposed asking the White House to send Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents and US Marshals to Maine polling locations ahead of the midterm elections.His defeat comes as Democrats make significant gains across the country, turning the 2026 midterms into a major political setback for Trump and the Republican Party.
